title: The Science of English Verse
description: Published in 1880 and the founding work of American prosody: an attempt to reduce English verse to the laws of music.
plot_or_argument: Lanier argues that verse is a form of music: that the rhythms of English poetry can be analysed in musical notation, that stress, quantity and pitch combine in a system of bars and notes, and that the whole history of English verse can be read as a series of musical arrangements of the same materials.
historical_context: 1880: the new science of acoustics, the American study of prosody after Lowell, the musical training of the period, and the professionalisation of literary study in the American university.
literary_significance: The Science of English Verse is the founding work of American prosody and the most original English-language theory of verse of the century: its musical analysis of metre influenced Pound, Eliot and the whole modern study of versification, and it remains the starting point of any serious discussion of English rhythm.

title: Poems (Lanier, 1877)
description: Published in 1877 and Lanier's first collection: the Southern lyrics, the war poems and the poems of music.
plot_or_argument: The volume gathers the poems of the Georgia countryside, the war poems written during and after the Confederate service, and the poems on music and on the trade of poetry, in forms that show Lanier's gift for long, musical lines and for the orchestration of a whole poem.
historical_context: 1867-77: the post-war South, the American magazine market of the 1870s, and the revival of Southern letters after Reconstruction.
literary_significance: Poems established Lanier as the finest Southern poet of the post-war generation: its lyrics of the Georgia landscape and its poems of music made him a national figure, and it prepared the way for the great poems of 1878-81.

title: The English Novel
description: Published posthumously in 1883 and Lanier's lectures on the history of the English novel: a formalist account of the development of fiction.
plot_or_argument: Lanier traces the English novel from its origins in the romance through Fielding, Richardson, Scott, Dickens, Thackeray and Eliot, arguing that the novel is a work of art with its own laws of structure, and that its greatness lies in the organisation of character and incident into a unified design.
historical_context: 1881-83: the American lecture circuit, the professional study of literature, and the Victorian debate on the art of fiction after James and Besant.
literary_significance: The English Novel is one of the earliest American works of formalist criticism of fiction and a landmark in the academic study of the novel: its lectures influenced the teaching of fiction in American universities, and it is the first American book to treat the novel as a serious art form.

title: The Old Swimmin'-Hole and 'Leven More Poems
description: Published in 1883 and the little book that made Riley the Hoosier Poet: twelve dialect poems of an Indiana boyhood.
plot_or_argument: The poems remember the swimming hole, the old schoolhouse, the country fair and the dead friends of a rural Indiana boyhood, in the Hoosier dialect of the 1850s and with a sentiment that made them instantly popular across the Midwest.
historical_context: 1882-83: rural Indiana, the small-town American Midwest of the 1850s, the newspaper poetry market, and the vogue of the dialect poem after Harte and Lowell.
literary_significance: The Old Swimmin'-Hole made Riley the most popular poet in America and founded the American dialect school of verse: its combination of exact speech and nostalgic recollection gave the Midwest a poetry of its own, and it sold in enormous numbers for decades.

title: Rhymes of Childhood
description: Published in 1890 and the collection containing 'Little Orphant Annie': the classic American poems of childhood.
plot_or_argument: The poems present the world of the Indiana child — the orphan girl who tells ghost stories, the boy at the swimming hole, the child at the window on Christmas Eve, the old couple and the grandchild — in dialect narratives that move from comedy to sentiment and back.
historical_context: 1885-90: the American small town of the 1880s, the children's market for recitation verse, and the vogue of the dialect poem in the schools.
literary_significance: Rhymes of Childhood contains 'Little Orphant Annie', the most famous American children's poem of the century and a permanent part of American popular culture: the collection made Riley the national poet of childhood, and it is the essential document of the American small-town imagination before the machine.

title: A Child-World
description: Published in 1896 and Riley's most sustained work: a sequence of poems on a single Indiana childhood and the town that surrounded it.
plot_or_argument: The sequence follows a boy and a girl through the seasons of a small-town childhood — the school, the church, the circus, the illness and death of a child, the first love and the departure — and ends with the town remembered by the grown man who has left it.
historical_context: 1895-96: the Indiana of the 1850s, the American small town before the railway and the factory, and the market for the nostalgic verse narrative.
literary_significance: A Child-World is Riley's most ambitious and most unified book: its sequence form and its elegiac tone made it something more than a collection of recitation pieces, and it is the finest American verse narrative of small-town childhood before Edgar Lee Masters.

title: Pipes o' Pan at Zekesbury
description: Published in 1889 and Riley's prose masterpiece: sketches of the Indiana town of Zekesbury and its characters.
plot_or_argument: The sketches present the inhabitants of a small Indiana town — the old soldier, the village doctor, the travelling salesman, the revivalist, the boy and the schoolteacher — in dialect narratives that are comic, affectionate and occasionally bitter, and that record a whole community.
historical_context: 1888-89: the Indiana small town of the 1880s, the American local-colour movement, and the newspaper sketch tradition of the Midwest.
literary_significance: Pipes o' Pan at Zekesbury is the finest American small-town sketchbook after Twain: its portraits and its dialect made it a landmark of the local-colour movement, and it is the book in which Riley's prose and his poetry are most completely united.

title: The Children of the Night
description: Published in 1897 and the book that founded modern American poetry: the first Tilbury Town poems and the lyrics of failure and endurance.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'Richard Cory', the rich man who goes home and puts a bullet through his head, 'Luke Havergal', the ghost-haunted lover, 'The House on the Hill', the abandoned house, and 'Credo', the poem of a faith that survives doubt, in plain, hard, traditional verse.
historical_context: 1896-97: the depression of 1893-97, the small New England town in decline, the American magazine poetry of the 1890s, and Robinson's own poverty in New York.
literary_significance: The Children of the Night is the founding book of modern American poetry: 'Richard Cory' became one of the most anthologised American poems, the Tilbury Town method changed the subject of American verse, and the collection made Robinson the first American poet to write modern poetry in traditional forms.

title: The Man against the Sky
description: Published in 1916 and the collection that established Robinson as a major poet: the title poem on the human figure against the void, and the Tilbury Town portraits.
plot_or_argument: The title poem presents the human being standing against the sky, face to face with the immensity and the indifference of the universe, and asks whether the courage to endure is not itself a kind of answer; the collection also contains 'Ben Jonson Entertains a Man from Stratford', 'Eros Turannos' and 'The Gift of God'.
historical_context: 1915-16: the First World War, the American reception of modernism, and the philosophical debate on the meaning of human existence after Darwin and Nietzsche.
literary_significance: The Man against the Sky made Robinson famous and is the finest single collection of American poetry of the 1910s: its title poem gave the age its image of human courage in an indifferent universe, and it confirmed Robinson's position as the leading American poet of his generation before the modernists.

title: Tristram
description: Published in 1927 and the Pulitzer Prize-winning climax of Robinson's Arthurian trilogy: the tragedy of Tristram and Isolt.
plot_or_argument: Tristram, wounded by a poisoned spear, sends for Isolt of Brittany, his wife, but asks for Isolt of Ireland, his love; the Irish Isolt comes too late, Tristram dies in her arms, and she dies on the shore as the ship brings her back to Brittany, in a retelling that strips the legend of its romance and leaves only the human cost.
historical_context: 1925-27: the American Arthurian revival of the 1920s, the aftermath of the First World War, and the modern scepticism about romantic love.
literary_significance: Tristram won the Pulitzer Prize in 1928 and is the finest American narrative poem of the century: its treatment of the Tristan legend as a study of human failure and its blank-verse music made it a landmark, and it completes the Arthurian trilogy that is Robinson's most ambitious work.

title: 'Richard Cory'
description: Published in 1897 and one of the most anthologised American poems ever written: the rich gentleman who is envied by the whole town and shoots himself.
plot_or_argument: The poem describes Richard Cory, the gentleman who is admired and envied by the people of the town, and then ends in two lines: 'And Richard Cory, one calm summer night, / Went home and put a bullet through his head.'
historical_context: 1896-97: the American small town of the 1890s, the depression of 1893-97, and the popular assumption that wealth brings happiness.
literary_significance: 'Richard Cory' is one of the most famous American poems of the century: its two-line reversal and its study of the gap between appearance and reality made it a permanent part of the American canon, it has been set to music and adapted many times, and it is the poem by which Robinson is most widely known.

title: Indian Boyhood
description: Published in 1902 and the classic Native American account of a traditional childhood: a Dakota boy's life on the plains and in the woods of Canada.
plot_or_argument: Ohiyesa remembers his Dakota boyhood: the games that trained him to hunt and to endure, the stories of the old people, the first buffalo hunt, the snowshoe journeys, the ceremonies and the moral education of a warrior, before he was taken at fifteen to be educated as a white man.
historical_context: 1860s-70s: the Santee Dakota after the 1862 uprising, the traditional life of the northern plains and the Canadian woods, and the American boarding-school policy of the 1870s.
literary_significance: Indian Boyhood is the classic Native American autobiography and one of the most widely read Native American books ever written: its account of a traditional Dakota childhood preserved a way of life that was disappearing, and it made Eastman the best-known Native American writer of his generation.

title: The Soul of the Indian
description: Published in 1911 and the foundational English account of Dakota religion: an interpretation of Native American spirituality for a white readership.
plot_or_argument: Eastman explains the Dakota belief in the Great Mystery, the practice of prayer and the vision quest, the reverence for the natural world and for the dead, and argues that the Native American religion is a form of natural monotheism closer to the spirit of Christianity than the white man's own conduct.
historical_context: 1911: the missionary campaign among Native Americans, the Society of American Indians, and the American debate on the assimilation and the 'vanishing race'.
literary_significance: The Soul of the Indian is the foundational English account of Native American religion and one of the most important Native American books of the century: its interpretation of Dakota spirituality shaped the white American understanding of Native religion, and it remains the classic statement of the Native American religious tradition.

title: From the Deep Woods to Civilization
description: Published in 1916 and the second volume of Eastman's autobiography: the passage from the Dakota world to Dartmouth, Boston and Wounded Knee.
plot_or_argument: Eastman recounts his father's return, his education at Beloit, Dartmouth and Boston University, his work as the physician at Pine Ridge, the massacre at Wounded Knee that he witnessed, and his later career as a writer and spokesman for the Native cause.
historical_context: 1873-1916: the assimilation policy of the 1880s, the Ghost Dance movement, the massacre at Wounded Knee in 1890, and the emergence of the Society of American Indians.
literary_significance: From the Deep Woods to Civilization is one of the most important Native American autobiographies and the central first-hand account of the massacre at Wounded Knee: its narrative of the passage between two worlds made it a classic, and it is the essential Native American document of the assimilation era.

title: Old Indian Days
description: Published in 1907 and Eastman's finest collection of stories: the warrior life of the Dakota before the reservation.
plot_or_argument: The stories follow the young Dakota men and women of the old life: the warrior who counts coup, the woman who follows the camp, the hunter, the medicine man and the lover, in narratives that record the code of honour and the daily life of the plains before the treaties.
historical_context: 1904-07: the last years of the free Dakota life, the reservation system, and the American market for the 'vanishing race' story.
literary_significance: Old Indian Days is the finest collection of Native American short stories of the period: its narratives of the warrior code and the daily life of the plains made it a classic, and it is one of the few Native-authored accounts of the old life written by someone who had lived it.

title: Sartor Resartus: The Life and Opinions of Herr Teufelsdröckh
description: Serialised in Fraser's Magazine in 1833-34 and published as a book in Boston in 1836 and in London in 1838: a 'clothes philosophy' in the form of an English editor's account of the German professor Diogenes Teufelsdröckh and his book on clothes, which becomes the spiritual autobiography of a modern soul.
plot_or_argument: The editor presents Teufelsdröckh's life and his 'Philosophy of Clothes', the doctrine that all institutions, creeds and customs are garments which time wears out. Teufelsdröckh's own history — the 'Everlasting No' of his despair, the 'Centre of Indifference', and the 'Everlasting Yea' of work and renunciation — is the model of the Victorian conversion narrative.
principal_characters: Diogenes Teufelsdröckh; the English editor; Hofrath Heuschrecke; Blumine; Herr Towgood; Gretchen
historical_context: German idealist philosophy (Fichte, Goethe, Kant) and the Scottish Calvinist background; the crisis of faith of the 1820s; and the Fraser's Magazine circle of the 1830s.
literary_significance: Sartor Resartus introduced German idealism to English readers and invented the modern spiritual autobiography of doubt and recovery; it was the single greatest influence on the Victorian literature of the 'Everlasting No', and Emerson's American edition of 1836 made Carlyle the intellectual hero of New England Transcendentalism.

title: The French Revolution: A History
description: Published in three volumes in 1837 after the manuscript of the first volume was accidentally burned by John Stuart Mill's housemaid: the greatest work of Victorian historiography and the book that made Carlyle famous.
plot_or_argument: The three parts — 'The Bastille', 'The Constitution', 'The Guillotine' — narrate the French Revolution from the death of Louis XV to the fall of Robespierre, by a method of vivid present-tense scenes, documents, portraits and choric commentary rather than by continuous analysis; the Revolution is presented as a terrible and necessary judgment on a corrupt society.
narrative_structure: Three parts of seven, five and seven books, in a loosely chronological sequence of scenes and portraits rather than an analytical argument.
literary_form: Historical prose narrative in three parts
historical_context: The 1830s and the memory of 1789 and 1830; Carlyle's reading of the French memoirs and pamphlets; and the British debate on reform that made the French Revolution a living political question.
literary_significance: The French Revolution changed the writing of history in English: its present-tense scenes, its documentary collage and its prophetic judgement created the modern literary history. Dickens used it as a source for A Tale of Two Cities, and its account of the Revolution as the work of 'the great dumb deep' shaped the Victorian and modern understanding of revolutionary politics.

title: On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History
description: Six lectures delivered in London in May 1840 and published in 1841: the most influential Victorian statement of the theory that history is the biography of great men, organised as six types of hero — the divinity (Odin), the prophet (Muhammad), the poet (Dante, Shakespeare), the priest (Luther, Knox), the man of letters (Johnson, Rousseau, Burns) and the king (Cromwell, Napoleon).
plot_or_argument: Each lecture presents its hero as the 'sincere' man who perceives the truth of his age and embodies it in action, and the sequence is an argument that the modern age, having lost its faith, finds its heroes in literature and in the 'man of letters'.
historical_context: The 1840 lecture season, the Chartist agitation of 1839-40, and the Victorian search for authority after the collapse of the old order; the lectures were attended by Dickens, Mill and the intellectual public of London.
literary_significance: On Heroes made hero-worship a central Victorian idea and supplied the age's theory of leadership; it shaped Carlyle's own Cromwell and Frederick, and Emerson's Representative Men, and its account of the man of letters as the modern priest gave Victorian authorship its sense of vocation. The twentieth century's reaction against its authoritarian implications made it the classic text for the critique of Victorian political thought.

title: Past and Present
description: Written in seven weeks in 1843 and the most concentrated of Carlyle's social criticisms: a comparison of the twelfth-century monastery of Bury St Edmunds, recovered from the chronicle of Jocelin of Brakelond, with the 'condition of England' in the Hungry Forties.
plot_or_argument: Book I, 'Proem', states the diagnosis of a society without a soul; Book II, 'The Ancient Monk', narrates Abbot Samson's governance of the monastery as a model of work and order; Book III, 'The Modern Worker', presents the 'Manchester insurrection', the 'Gospel of Work' and the parson and the priest of the modern world; Book IV, 'Horoscope', prophesies the consequences of the neglect of the poor.
historical_context: The Chartist riots of 1839-42, the 'Hungry Forties', the New Poor Law and the factory system, and the Victorian debate between laissez-faire and the duty of the state.
literary_significance: Past and Present is the founding text of Victorian social criticism and the source of much of the vocabulary of the later Labour movement; its 'Gospel of Work', its attack on the 'cash nexus' and its demand for a governing aristocracy of talent shaped Ruskin, Dickens, Kingsley, Morris and the Christian socialists, and it remains the classic English indictment of industrial capitalism from the right.

title: Chartism
description: Published in December 1839 at the height of the Chartist agitation and the most important contemporary analysis of it by an intellectual: an essay that takes the Charter seriously as a symptom of a deeper condition rather than as a programme.
plot_or_argument: Carlyle asks 'what the condition of England really is' and answers that Chartism is the symptom of the 'dyspepsia' of a society in which the working man has no voice, no leader and no hope; the remedy is not the ballot but the recognition of the duties of the governing class and the right of the worker to work.
historical_context: The Chartist petition of 1839, the Newport rising of November 1839, the Poor Law and the factory question; Carlyle's argument was delivered as the agitation reached its height.
literary_significance: Chartism invented the phrase 'the condition of England question' and set the terms of the Victorian social novel: Disraeli's Sybil, Gaskell's Mary Barton and Dickens's Hard Times all answer Carlyle's diagnosis, and it is the founding document of the critique of Victorian industrialism.

title: Oliver Cromwell's Letters and Speeches: with Elucidations
description: Published in 1845, and the work that rehabilitated Cromwell in the English historical imagination: the letters and speeches, edited with a commentary that presents Cromwell as the sincere Puritan hero and the founder of English liberty.
plot_or_argument: Carlyle arranges the documents chronologically from the 1620s to Cromwell's death in 1658, with 'elucidations' that supply narrative and argument; the effect is a first-person portrait of the man in his own words, from the fen drainage and the Irish campaign to the Protectorate and the deathbed.
historical_context: The 1840s and the Victorian interest in the Puritan past, the edition of the letters by Carlyle's friend Thomas Carlyle and the earlier editions of the Thurloe papers, and the 1841-42 controversy over Cromwell's statue.
literary_significance: Cromwell's Letters and Speeches made Cromwell a Victorian hero and established the documentary edition as a form of historical writing; it shaped Froude's and Gardiner's histories and the modern scholarly edition, and it is the classic example of Carlyle's method of letting a man speak for himself.

title: The Life of John Sterling
description: Published in 1851, Carlyle's brief and moving biography of his friend John Sterling, the Irish-born writer and clergyman who moved from Coleridgean idealism through the Oxford Movement to a free-thinking Christianity and died at forty.
plot_or_argument: Carlyle follows Sterling's life from Cambridge and the Apostles through his marriage, his colonial venture in the West Indies, his editorship of the Athenaeum, his friendship with Carlyle and his final years of illness and religious searching, quoting the letters and setting them in the narrative.
historical_context: The 1830s-40s, the Oxford Movement, the Athenaeum, and the Victorian crisis of faith as it appeared in an individual life.
literary_significance: The Life of John Sterling is the finest of Carlyle's shorter biographies and a central document of Victorian friendship and religious doubt; it is also the model for the Victorian life-and-letters biography that Gaskell's Brontë and Froude's Carlyle later practised.

title: History of Friedrich II of Prussia, called Frederick the Great
description: Published in six volumes between 1858 and 1865, the last and longest of Carlyle's works, and the most ambitious Victorian attempt to write the history of an age through the biography of a king.
plot_or_argument: The history follows Frederick from his brutal upbringing under Frederick William I through the Silesian wars, the Seven Years' War and the partition of Poland to his death in 1786, with long digressions on the German princes, the Prussian army and the diplomacy of the eighteenth century.
historical_context: The 1850s-60s, the Crimean War and the rise of Prussia, and the Victorian admiration for German culture and efficiency.
literary_significance: Frederick the Great is Carlyle's masterpiece of narrative history and one of the great monuments of Victorian prose; it made the eighteenth century live for English readers and established the narrative-history method that Macaulay and Froude practised, and its admiration for Prussian order shaped Victorian and later attitudes to Germany.

title: Modern Painters
description: Begun in 1843 as a defence of J. M. W. Turner under the anonymous title 'by a Graduate of Oxford' and completed in 1860 in five volumes: the most ambitious work of art criticism in English, moving from the truth of landscape painting to a complete theory of the imagination and of the relation of art to religion.
plot_or_argument: Volume I defends Turner's truth to nature against the critics; Volume II (1846) develops the theory of the beautiful and the 'pathetic fallacy' and the classification of the 'theoretic' and 'imaginative' faculties; Volumes III-V (1856-60) treat the symbolism of landscape, the Renaissance and the relation of art to the moral and religious state of the artist's age.
historical_context: The 1840s and the Turner controversy, the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood of 1848 (which Ruskin defended in 1851), the growth of the Victorian art market, and Ruskin's own travels in Italy and Switzerland.
literary_significance: Modern Painters established Ruskin as the leading art critic of the century and made Turner a national painter; it introduced the 'pathetic fallacy' into criticism, gave the Pre-Raphaelites their critical defence, and turned art criticism into a branch of moral philosophy that Pater and Wilde had to answer.

title: The Seven Lamps of Architecture
description: Published in 1849 with Ruskin's own etchings, and the first statement of the moral theory of architecture: the seven lamps of Sacrifice, Truth, Power, Beauty, Life, Memory and Obedience.
plot_or_argument: Each lamp is a principle tested against buildings old and new; the lamp of Truth condemns the imitation of materials and the restoration of ancient buildings; the lamp of Memory makes buildings the record of a nation's past; the lamp of Obedience argues for the authority of tradition in architecture.
historical_context: The Victorian Gothic Revival, the restoration controversies of the 1840s (the 'Anti-Scrape' campaign Ruskin later supported), and the railway and industrial building of the period.
literary_significance: The Seven Lamps founded the moral criticism of architecture and the Victorian Gothic Revival's intellectual programme; its attack on restoration led directly to William Morris's Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings (1877), and its seven principles became the vocabulary of the Arts and Crafts movement.
